claim: Metabolic syndrome (MetS) represents a cluster of cardiometabolic risk factors, including abdominal obesity, arterial hypertension, dyslipidemia, and insulin resistance.
source: Metabolic syndrome (MetS) represents a cluster of cardiometabolic risk factors, including abdominal obesity, arterial hypertension, dyslipidemia, and insulin resistance (Alberti et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Alberti et al., 2006, which is a reference to established scientific literature defining metabolic syndrome.

claim: The prevalence of metabolic syndrome is 23–35% in Western societies.
source: With a prevalence of 23–35% in Western societies, it poses a considerable health challenge, promoting neurodegenerative, and cerebrovascular diseases such as cognitive decline, dementia, and stroke (Aguilar et al., 2015; Scuteri et al., 2015; Beltrán-Sánchez et al., 2013; Boden-Albala et al., 2008; Atti et al., 2019).
evidence: The prevalence range is supported by multiple citations to epidemiological studies (Aguilar et al., 2015; Scuteri et al., 2015; Beltrán-Sánchez et al., 2013).

claim: Metabolic syndrome promotes neurodegenerative and cerebrovascular diseases such as cognitive decline, dementia, and stroke.
source: With a prevalence of 23–35% in Western societies, it poses a considerable health challenge, promoting neurodegenerative, and cerebrovascular diseases such as cognitive decline, dementia, and stroke (Aguilar et al., 2015; Scuteri et al., 2015; Beltrán-Sánchez et al., 2013; Boden-Albala et al., 2008; Atti et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to studies linking MetS to neurological diseases (Aguilar et al., 2015; Scuteri et al., 2015; Beltrán-Sánchez et al., 2013; Boden-Albala et al., 2008; Atti et al., 2019).

claim: Lifestyle and pharmacological interventions can modify the trajectory of metabolic syndrome.
source: As lifestyle and pharmacological interventions can modify the trajectory of MetS, advancing our understanding of its pathophysiological effects on brain structure and function as potential mediators of MetS-related neurological diseases is crucial to inform and motivate risk reduction strategies (Eckel et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Eckel et al., 2005, which discusses interventions for metabolic syndrome.

claim: Alterations in cortical gray matter morphology are one of the most consistent findings in studies exploring MetS and brain structure.
source: Among studies exploring MetS and brain structure, one of the most consistent findings has been alterations in cortical gray matter morphology (Yates et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Yates et al., 2012, which reviews findings on MetS and brain structure.

claim: The study investigated cortical thickness and subcortical volumetric measurements in a pooled sample of 40,087 participants from the UK Biobank and Hamburg City Health Study.
source: To meet these research needs, we investigated cortical thickness and subcortical volumetric measurements in a pooled sample of two large-scale population-based cohorts from the UK Biobank (UKB) and Hamburg City Health Study (HCHS) comprising in total 40,087 participants.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the manuscript and describes the study sample and measurements.

claim: Partial least squares correlation analysis (PLS) was employed to characterize MetS effects on regional brain morphology.
source: Partial least squares correlation analysis (PLS) was employed to characterize MetS effects on regional brain morphology.
evidence: The claim describes the statistical method used in the study as stated in the manuscript.

claim: Application of exclusion criteria and quality assessment ruled out 2188 UKB subjects and 30 HCHS subjects resulting in a final analysis sample of 40,087 individuals.
source: Application of exclusion criteria and quality assessment ruled out 2188 UKB subjects and 30 HCHS subjects resulting in a final analysis sample of 40,087 individuals.
evidence: The claim describes the sample selection process and final sample size as reported in the Results section.

claim: PLS identified eight significant latent variables which represent clinical-anatomical dimensions relating MetS components to brain morphology.
source: PLS identified eight significant latent variables which represent clinical-anatomical dimensions relating MetS components to brain morphology (Appendix 1—table 1).
evidence: The claim reports a finding from the PLS analysis with reference to a table showing the results.

claim: The first latent variable explained 71.20% of the shared variance.
source: The first latent variable explained 71.20% of the shared variance and was thus further investigated (Figure 2a).
evidence: The claim reports a quantitative result from the PLS analysis shown in Figure 2a.

claim: The first latent variable corresponded with a covariance profile of lower severity of MetS.
source: Specifically, the first latent variable corresponded with a covariance profile of lower severity of MetS (Figure 2c; loadings [95% confidence interval]; waist circumference: –0.230 [–0.239, –0.221], hip circumference: –0.187 [–0.195, –0.178], waist-hip ratio: –0.167 [–0.176, –0.158], body mass index: –0.234 [–0.243, –0.226], systolic blood pressure: –0.089 [–0.098, –0.080], diastolic blood pressure: –0.116 [–0.125, –0.107], high-density lipoprotein: 0.099 [0.090, 0.108], low-density lipoprotein: –0.013 [–0.022, –0.004], total cholesterol: 0.003 [–0.006, 0.012], triglycerides: –0.102 [–0.111, –0.092], HbA1c: –0.064 [–0.073, –0.54], glucose: –0.049 [–0.058, –0.039]).
evidence: The claim reports the covariance profile with specific loading values and confidence intervals from the PLS analysis, shown in Figure 2c.

claim: Obesity-related measures showed the strongest contribution to the covariance profile as indicated by the highest loading to the latent variable.
source: Notably, the obesity-related measures showed the strongest contribution to the covariance profile as indicated by the highest loading to the latent variable.
evidence: The claim is based on the loading values reported in the PLS analysis, where obesity measures had the highest absolute values.

claim: Age, sex, education, and cohort did not significantly contribute to the first latent variable.
source: Age (<0.001 [–0.009, 0.009]), sex (<0.001 [–0.009, 0.009]), education (<0.001 [–0.009, 0.009]), and cohort (<–0.001 [–0.008, 0.007]) did not significantly contribute to the latent variable, which is compatible with sufficient effects of deconfounding.
evidence: The claim reports loading values with confidence intervals that include zero, indicating no significant contribution after deconfounding.

claim: The second latent variable explained 22.33% of shared variance.
source: Details on the second latent variable which explained 22.33% of shared variance are provided in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.
evidence: The claim reports a quantitative result from the PLS analysis with reference to a supplementary figure.

claim: The second latent variable predominantly related lower HbA1c and blood glucose to higher thickness and volume in lateral frontal, posterior temporal, parietal, and occipital regions.
source: In brief, it predominantly related lower HbA1c and blood glucose to higher thickness and volume in lateral frontal, posterior temporal, parietal, and occipital regions and vice versa.
evidence: The claim summarizes the relationship identified in the second latent variable from the PLS analysis.

claim: Cortical thickness in orbitofrontal, lateral prefrontal, insular, anterior cingulate, and temporal areas as well as volumes of all investigated subcortical regions contributed positively to the covariance profile.
source: Cortical thickness in orbitofrontal, lateral prefrontal, insular, anterior cingulate, and temporal areas as well as volumes of all investigated subcortical regions contributed positively to the covariance profile as indicated by a positive bootstrap ratio (Figure 2d).
evidence: The claim reports findings from the bootstrap ratio analysis shown in Figure 2d.

claim: Higher cortical thickness and subcortical volume in orbitofrontal, lateral prefrontal, insular, anterior cingulate, and temporal areas corresponded with less obesity, hypertension, dyslipidemia, and insulin resistance.
source: Thus, a higher cortical thickness and subcortical volume in these areas corresponded with less obesity, hypertension, dyslipidemia, and insulin resistance and vice versa, i.e., lower cortical thickness and subcortical volumes with increased severity of MetS.
evidence: The claim interprets the positive bootstrap ratio findings in terms of the relationship between brain structure and MetS severity.

claim: A negative bootstrap ratio was found in superior frontal, parietal, and occipital regions indicating that a higher cortical thickness in these regions corresponded with more severe MetS.
source: A negative bootstrap ratio was found in superior frontal, parietal, and occipital regions indicating that a higher cortical thickness in these regions corresponded with more severe MetS.
evidence: The claim reports findings from the bootstrap ratio analysis showing a counterintuitive positive association.

claim: The overall pattern was confirmed via conventional, vertex-wise group comparisons of cortical thickness measurements based on the binary classification of individuals with MetS and matched controls.
source: This overall pattern was confirmed via conventional, vertex-wise group comparisons of cortical thickness measurements based on the binary classification of individuals with MetS and matched controls (Appendix 2—figure 4) as well as subsample analyses considering the UKB and HCHS participants independently (Figure 2—figure supplements 2 and 3).
evidence: The claim reports that the PLS findings were validated using a different analytical approach (group comparisons).

claim: The imaging score fully mediated the relationship of the clinical score and results of the Trail Making Test B.
source: The imaging score was found to fully mediate the relationship of the clinical score and results of the Trail Making Test B (ab = –0.011, PFDR <0.001; c'=–0.012, PFDR = 0.072; c=–0.023, PFDR <0.001)
evidence: The claim reports specific mediation analysis results with effect sizes and p-values indicating full mediation.

claim: The imaging score fully mediated the relationship of the clinical score and Fluid Intelligence Test results.
source: Fluid Intelligence Test (ab = 0.017, PFDR <0.001; c'=0.011, PFDR = 0.072; c=0.028, PFDR <0.001)
evidence: The claim reports mediation analysis results showing full mediation for the Fluid Intelligence Test.

claim: The imaging score fully mediated the relationship of the clinical score and Matrix Pattern Completion Test results.
source: as well as Matrix Pattern Completion Test (ab = 0.015, PFDR <0.001; c'=0.010, PFDR = 0.172; c=0.025, PFDR <0.001).
evidence: The claim reports mediation analysis results showing full mediation for the Matrix Pattern Completion Test.

claim: The imaging score partially mediated the relationship of the clinical score and Symbol Digit Substitution Test results.
source: Further, the imaging score partially mediated the relationship of the clinical score and results of the Symbol Digit Substitution Test (ab = 0.010, PFDR <0.001; c'=0.036, PFDR <0.001; c=0.046, PFDR <0.001)
evidence: The claim reports mediation analysis results showing partial mediation for the Symbol Digit Substitution Test.

claim: The imaging score partially mediated the relationship of the clinical score and Numeric Memory Test results.
source: Numeric Memory Test (ab = 0.014, PFDR <0.001; c'=0.044, PFDR <0.001; c=0.058, PFDR <0.001)
evidence: The claim reports mediation analysis results showing partial mediation for the Numeric Memory Test.

claim: The imaging score partially mediated the relationship of the clinical score and Paired Associate Learning Test results.
source: and Paired Associate Learning Test (ab = 0.015, PFDR <0.001; c'=0.044, PFDR <0.001; c=0.059, PFDR <0.001).
evidence: The claim reports mediation analysis results showing partial mediation for the Paired Associate Learning Test.

claim: MetS-related brain morphological abnormalities are strongest in regions of the highest density of endothelial cells, microglia, excitatory neurons type 8, inhibitory neurons type 1, and excitatory neurons type 6.
source: indicating that MetS-related brain morphological abnormalities are strongest in regions of the highest density of these cell types.
evidence: The claim interprets the correlation results from the virtual histology analysis in terms of regional susceptibility to MetS effects.

claim: Functional and structural interconnectedness of areas exhibiting similar MetS effects was indicated by the correlation with neighborhood abnormality.
source: indicating functional and structural interconnectedness of areas exhibiting similar MetS effects.
evidence: The claim interprets the neighborhood abnormality correlation results in terms of network connectivity patterns.

claim: Multivariate, data-driven statistics identified a latent dimension linking more severe MetS to widespread brain morphological abnormalities, accounting for up to 71% of shared variance in the data.
source: Multivariate, data-driven statistics identified a latent dimension linking more severe MetS to widespread brain morphological abnormalities, accounting for up to 71% of shared variance in the data.
evidence: The claim summarizes a main finding from the PLS analysis reported in the Abstract.

claim: The latent dimension was replicable across sub-samples.
source: This dimension was replicable across sub-samples.
evidence: The claim reports the replicability of the main finding across UKB and HCHS subsamples.

claim: MetS-related brain morphological abnormalities mediated the link between MetS severity and cognitive performance in multiple domains.
source: In a mediation analysis, we could demonstrate that MetS-related brain morphological abnormalities mediated the link between MetS severity and cognitive performance in multiple domains.
evidence: The claim summarizes the mediation analysis findings reported in the Abstract.

claim: MetS-related morphological abnormalities are linked to the regional cellular composition.
source: Employing imaging transcriptomics and connectomics, our results also suggest that MetS-related morphological abnormalities are linked to the regional cellular composition and macroscopic brain network organization.
evidence: The claim summarizes findings from the contextualization analyses reported in the Abstract.

claim: MetS-related morphological abnormalities are linked to macroscopic brain network organization.
source: Employing imaging transcriptomics and connectomics, our results also suggest that MetS-related morphological abnormalities are linked to the regional cellular composition and macroscopic brain network organization.
evidence: The claim summarizes findings from the contextualization analyses reported in the Abstract.

claim: The pathophysiology of MetS involves atherosclerosis, which affects blood supply and triggers inflammation.
source: The pathophysiology of MetS involves atherosclerosis, which affects blood supply and triggers inflammation (Libby et al., 2002; Birdsill et al., 2013)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies on MetS pathophysiology (Libby et al., 2002; Birdsill et al., 2013).

claim: The pathophysiology of MetS involves endothelial dysfunction reducing cerebral vasoreactivity.
source: endothelial dysfunction reducing cerebral vasoreactivity Lind, 2008
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lind, 2008, discussing endothelial dysfunction in MetS.

claim: The pathophysiology of MetS involves breakdown of the blood-brain barrier inciting an inflammatory response.
source: breakdown of the blood-brain barrier inciting an inflammatory response Hussain et al., 2021
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hussain et al., 2021, discussing blood-brain barrier breakdown in MetS.

claim: The pathophysiology of MetS involves oxidative stress causing neuronal and mitochondrial dysfunction.
source: oxidative stress causing neuronal and mitochondrial dysfunction Mullins et al., 2020
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Mullins et al., 2020, discussing oxidative stress in MetS.

claim: The pathophysiology of MetS involves small vessel injury leading to various pathologies including white matter damage, microinfarcts, and cerebral microbleeds.
source: and small vessel injury leading to various pathologies including white matter damage, microinfarcts, and cerebral microbleeds (Frey et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Frey et al., 2019, discussing small vessel injury in MetS.

claim: All MetS components were contributing to the latent signature identified by PLS.
source: PLS revealed that all MetS components were contributing to this latent signature.
evidence: The claim summarizes the PLS results showing that all MetS components had non-zero loadings on the first latent variable.

claim: Waist circumference, hip circumference, waist-hip ratio, and body mass index consistently contributed higher than the remaining variables across conducted analyses.
source: However, waist circumference, hip circumference, waist-hip ratio, and body mass index consistently contributed higher than the remaining variables across conducted analyses which highlights obesity as the strongest driver of MetS-related brain morphological abnormalities.
evidence: The claim is based on the loading values from the PLS analysis showing obesity measures had the highest contributions.

claim: Obesity is the strongest driver of MetS-related brain morphological abnormalities.
source: which highlights obesity as the strongest driver of MetS-related brain morphological abnormalities.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the PLS loading values showing obesity measures had the highest contributions.

claim: MetS-associated conditions jointly contribute to the harmful effects on brain structure rather than affecting it in a strictly individual manner.
source: We interpret these findings as evidence that MetS-associated conditions jointly contribute to the harmful effects on brain structure rather than affecting it in a strictly individual manner.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the PLS results showing all MetS components contribute to a shared latent dimension.

claim: Previous work in the UKB demonstrated overlapping effects of individual risk factors on brain morphology.
source: This notion is supported by previous work in the UKB demonstrating overlapping effects of individual risk factors on brain morphology (Cox et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Cox et al., 2019, which reported overlapping effects of risk factors.

claim: The first latent variable related increased severity of obesity, dyslipidemia, arterial hypertension, and insulin resistance with lower thickness in orbitofrontal, lateral prefrontal, insular, cingulate, and temporal cortices as well as lower volume across subcortical regions.
source: Specifically, the first latent variable related to increased severity of obesity, dyslipidemia, arterial hypertension, and insulin resistance with lower thickness in orbitofrontal, lateral prefrontal, insular, cingulate, and temporal cortices as well as lower volume across subcortical regions (Figure 2c and d).
evidence: The claim summarizes the relationship identified in the first latent variable from the PLS analysis, shown in Figures 2c and 2d.

claim: Previous research aligns with the detection of a MetS-associated frontotemporal morphometric abnormality pattern.
source: Previous research aligns with our detection of a MetS-associated frontotemporal morphometric abnormality pattern (Beyer et al., 2019; McIntosh et al., 2017; Kotkowski et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Beyer et al., 2019; McIntosh et al., 2017; Kotkowski et al., 2019) that reported similar patterns.

claim: Human and animal studies have related the orbitofrontal, insular, and anterior cingulate cortex to food-related reward processing, taste, and impulse regulation.
source: As a speculative causative pathway, human and animal studies have related the orbitofrontal, insular, and anterior cingulate cortex to food-related reward processing, taste, and impulse regulation (Tuulari et al., 2015; Rolls, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies (Tuulari et al., 2015; Rolls, 2016) linking these brain regions to food-related behaviors.

claim: Structural alterations of orbitofrontal, insular, and anterior cingulate cortex might be linked to brain functions and behaviors that exacerbate the risk profile leading to MetS.
source: Conceivably, structural alterations of these brain regions are linked to brain functions and behaviors that exacerbate the risk profile leading to MetS (Rolls, 2023; Price et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is a speculative interpretation supported by citations to studies (Rolls, 2023; Price et al., 2019) on brain-behavior relationships.

claim: A positive MetS-cortical thickness association in superior frontal, parietal, and occipital lobes has been previously reported.
source: We also noted a positive MetS-cortical thickness association in superior frontal, parietal, and occipital lobes, a less intuitive finding that has been previously reported (Krishnadas et al., 2013; Leritz et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Krishnadas et al., 2013; Leritz et al., 2011) that reported similar positive associations.

claim: The positive effects might be due to MetS compensating cholesterol disruptions associated with neurodegenerative processes.
source: Although speculative, the positive effects might be due to MetS compensating cholesterol disruptions associated with neurodegenerative processes (Qin et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is a speculative interpretation supported by a citation to Qin et al., 2021, discussing cholesterol in neurodegeneration.

claim: The second latent variable linked higher markers of insulin resistance and lower dyslipidemia to lower thickness and volume in lateral frontal, posterior temporal, parietal, and occipital regions.
source: The second latent variable accounted for 22.33% of the shared variance and linked higher markers of insulin resistance and lower dyslipidemia to lower thickness and volume in lateral frontal, posterior temporal, parietal, and occipital regions.
evidence: The claim summarizes the relationship identified in the second latent variable from the PLS analysis.

claim: The distinct covariance profile of the second latent variable likely indicates a separate pathomechanistic connection between MetS components and brain morphology.
source: The distinct covariance profile of this latent variable, compared to the first, likely indicates a separate pathomechanistic connection between MetS components and brain morphology.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the PLS results showing a distinct pattern in the second latent variable.

claim: Insulin resistance might drive the clinical-anatomical relationship observed in the second latent variable.
source: Given that HbA1c and blood glucose were the most significant contributors to this variable, insulin resistance might drive the observed clinical-anatomical relationship.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation based on the loading values in the second latent variable showing HbA1c and glucose had the highest contributions.

claim: Cognitive performance has been consistently linked to cardiometabolic risk factors in health and disease.
source: Cognitive performance has been consistently linked to cardiometabolic risk factors in health and disease (Genon et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Genon et al., 2022, which reviews the link between cognition and cardiometabolic risk.

claim: Increased MetS severity correlates with worse performance in executive function and processing speed, memory, and reasoning.
source: Our mediation analysis revealed that increased MetS severity correlates with worse performance in executive function and processing speed (Symbol Digit Substitution Test, Trail Making Test B), memory (Numeric Memory Test, Paired Associate Learning Test), and reasoning (Fluid intelligence, Matrix Pattern Completion Test), with brain morphological abnormalities statistically mediating these relationships.
evidence: The claim summarizes the mediation analysis results showing correlations between MetS severity and cognitive performance.

claim: Brain morphological abnormalities statistically mediate the relationship between MetS severity and cognitive performance.
source: with brain morphological abnormalities statistically mediating these relationships.
evidence: The claim summarizes the mediation analysis results showing brain structure as a mediator.

claim: Group comparisons indicated poorer cognitive performance in MetS subjects.
source: Additionally, group comparisons indicated poorer cognitive performance in MetS subjects (Appendix 2—tables 1 and 2)
evidence: The claim reports findings from group comparisons with reference to appendix tables.

claim: Including cognitive outcomes in the PLS as clinical variables revealed a significant contribution to the first latent variable.
source: and including cognitive outcomes in the PLS as clinical variables revealed a significant contribution to the first latent variable (Figure 2—figure supplements 2 and 3).
evidence: The claim reports findings from subsample PLS analyses shown in supplementary figures.

claim: MetS is significantly associated with cognitive deficits across various domains.
source: These results suggest that MetS is significantly associated with cognitive deficits across various domains, and brain morphological abnormalities are a crucial pathomechanistic link in this relationship.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the mediation analysis and PLS results showing associations between MetS and cognition.

claim: Brain morphological abnormalities are a crucial pathomechanistic link in the relationship between MetS and cognitive deficits.
source: and brain morphological abnormalities are a crucial pathomechanistic link in this relationship.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the mediation analysis results showing brain structure mediates the MetS-cognition relationship.

claim: Previous studies have shown that brain structure mediates the relationship between MetS and cognitive performance in a pediatric sample and elderly patients with vascular cognitive impairment.
source: In support of this, previous studies have shown that brain structure mediates the relationship between MetS and cognitive performance in a pediatric sample and elderly patients with vascular cognitive impairment (Laurent et al., 2020; Seo et al., 2010; Kim et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Laurent et al., 2020; Seo et al., 2010; Kim et al., 2014) showing similar mediation effects.

claim: The detected latent variable might represent a continuous disease spectrum spanning from minor cognitive deficits due to a cardiometabolic risk profile to severe cognitive deficits due to dementia.
source: The detected latent variable might represent a continuous disease spectrum spanning from minor cognitive deficits due to a cardiometabolic risk profile to severe cognitive deficits due to dementia.
evidence: The claim is a speculative interpretation of the PLS results suggesting a disease continuum.

claim: The determined brain morphological abnormality pattern is consistent with the atrophy pattern found in vascular mild cognitive impairment, vascular dementia, and Alzheimer's dementia.
source: In support of this hypothesis, the determined brain morphological abnormality pattern is consistent with the atrophy pattern found in vascular mild cognitive impairment, vascular dementia, and Alzheimer's dementia (Seo et al., 2010; Kim et al., 2014; Morys et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies (Seo et al., 2010; Kim et al., 2014; Morys et al., 2023) showing similar atrophy patterns in dementia.

claim: Emerging evidence suggests that interventions targeting cardiometabolic risk factors can mitigate the adverse cognitive effects of MetS.
source: Although the definitive role of such therapies in preventing cognitive decline is not yet fully established, emerging evidence suggests that these interventions can mitigate the adverse cognitive effects of MetS (Veronese et al., 2017; Lennon et al., 2023; Gelber et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies (Veronese et al., 2017; Lennon et al., 2023; Gelber et al., 2013) on interventions for MetS and cognition.

claim: Higher MetS-related brain morphological abnormalities coincide with a higher regional density of endothelial cells.
source: As the main finding, we report that higher MetS-related brain morphological abnormalities coincide with a higher regional density of endothelial cells.
evidence: The claim summarizes the main finding from the virtual histology analysis.

claim: The association between MetS effects and endothelial density aligns with the known role of endothelial dysfunction in MetS compromising tissues via chronic vascular inflammation, increased thrombosis risk, and hypoperfusion.
source: This aligns with the known role of endothelial dysfunction in MetS compromising tissues via chronic vascular inflammation, increased thrombosis risk, and hypoperfusion due to altered vasoreactivity and vascular remodeling (Lind, 2008).
evidence: The claim interprets the virtual histology results in the context of known MetS pathophysiology, supported by a citation to Lind, 2008.

claim: Endothelial density indicates the degree of general tissue vascularization.
source: As endothelial density also indicates the degree of general tissue vascularization, well-vascularized regions are also likely more exposed to cardiometabolic risk factor effects in general (Libby et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is an interpretation supported by a citation to Libby et al., 2002, discussing vascular exposure to risk factors.

claim: Microglial density determines a brain region's susceptibility to MetS effects.
source: Our results furthermore indicate that microglial density determines a brain region's susceptibility to MetS effects.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the virtual histology results showing correlation with microglial density.

claim: Animal studies have linked microglial activation mediated by blood-brain barrier leakage and systemic inflammation to cardiometabolic risk.
source: Animal studies have linked microglial activation mediated by blood-brain barrier leakage and systemic inflammation to cardiometabolic risk (Denes et al., 2012; Tucsek et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to animal studies (Denes et al., 2012; Tucsek et al., 2014) on microglial activation in cardiometabolic risk.

claim: Activated microglia can harm the brain structure by releasing reactive oxygen species, proinflammatory cytokines, and proteinases.
source: Activated microglia can harm the brain structure by releasing reactive oxygen species, proinflammatory cytokines, and proteinases (Dheen et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Dheen et al., 2007, discussing mechanisms of microglial-mediated damage.

claim: Excitatory neurons of subtype 8 reside in cortical layer 6 and their axons mainly entertain long-range cortico-cortical and cortico-thalamic connections.
source: These neurons reside in cortical layer 6 and their axons mainly entertain long-range cortico-cortical and cortico-thalamic connections (Lake et al., 2016; Thomson, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies (Lake et al., 2016; Thomson, 2010) on the properties of layer 6 excitatory neurons.

claim: Layer 6 neurons might be particularly susceptible to MetS effects due to their exposition to MetS-related white matter disease.
source: Consequently, layer 6 neurons might be particularly susceptible to MetS effects due to their exposition to MetS-related white matter disease (Petersen et al., 2022a; Petersen et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is a speculative interpretation supported by citations to studies (Petersen et al., 2022a; Petersen et al., 2020) on MetS-related white matter disease.

claim: The virtual histology analysis indicates that MetS-related brain morphological abnormalities are associated with local cellular fingerprints.
source: Taken together, the virtual histology analysis indicates that MetS-related brain morphological abnormalities are associated with local cellular fingerprints.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation summarizing the virtual histology analysis results.

claim: The findings emphasize the involvement of endothelial cells and microglia in brain structural abnormalities due to cardiometabolic risk.
source: Our findings emphasize the involvement of endothelial cells and microglia in brain structural abnormalities due to cardiometabolic risk, marking them as potential targets for therapies aimed at mitigating MetS effects on brain health.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the virtual histology results with implications for therapeutic targets.

claim: Regional MetS effects and those of functionally and structurally connected neighbors were correlated.
source: We found that regional MetS effects and those of functionally and structurally connected neighbors were correlated (Figure 5c and d) – i.e., areas with similar MetS effects tended to be disproportionately interconnected.
evidence: The claim reports findings from the network topology analysis shown in Figures 5c and 5d.

claim: Areas with similar MetS effects tended to be disproportionately interconnected.
source: i.e., areas with similar MetS effects tended to be disproportionately interconnected.
evidence: The claim interprets the neighborhood abnormality correlation results in terms of network connectivity.

claim: MetS effects coincided within functional and structural brain networks.
source: Put differently, MetS effects coincided within functional and structural brain networks.
evidence: The claim is an alternative interpretation of the neighborhood abnormality correlation results.

claim: A region's functional and structural network embedding is associated with its susceptibility to morphological MetS effects.
source: Therefore, our findings can be interpreted as evidence that a region's functional and structural network embedding – i.e., its individual profile of functional interactions as well as white matter fiber tract connections – are associated with its susceptibility to morphological MetS effects.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the network topology analysis results.

claim: Microvascular pathology might impair white matter fiber tracts leading to joint degeneration in interconnected cortical brain areas.
source: For example, microvascular pathology might impair white matter fiber tracts leading to joint degeneration in interconnected cortical brain areas: that is, the occurrence of shared MetS effects within functionally and structurally connected neighborhoods is explained by their shared (dis-)connectivity profile (Mayer et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is a speculative mechanistic interpretation supported by a citation to Mayer et al., 2021.

claim: Previous work using diffusion tensor imaging suggests that MetS-related microstructural white matter alterations preferentially occur in the frontal and temporal lobe.
source: In support of this, previous work using diffusion tensor imaging suggests that MetS-related microstructural white matter alterations preferentially occur in the frontal and temporal lobe, which spatially matches the frontotemporal morphometric differences observed in our work (Segura et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Segura et al., 2009, which reported white matter alterations in MetS.

claim: Functional and structural connectivity may provide a scaffold for propagating MetS-related perturbation across the network in the sense of a spreading phenomenon.
source: Furthermore, we speculate on an interplay between local and network-topological susceptibility in MetS: functional and structural connectivity may provide a scaffold for propagating MetS-related perturbation across the network in the sense of a spreading phenomenon – i.e., a region might be influenced by network-driven exposure to regions with higher local susceptibility.
evidence: The claim is a speculative interpretation of the network topology results proposing a spreading mechanism.

claim: Observed degeneration of a region might be aggravated by malfunctional communication to other vulnerable regions including mechanisms of excitotoxicity, diminished excitation and metabolic stress.
source: Observed degeneration of a region might be aggravated by malfunctional communication to other vulnerable regions including mechanisms of excitotoxicity, diminished excitation and metabolic stress (Saxena and Caroni, 2011).
evidence: The claim is a speculative interpretation supported by a citation to Saxena and Caroni, 2011, discussing network-mediated degeneration mechanisms.

claim: The findings underscore the relevance of brain network organization in understanding the pathomechanistic link of MetS and brain morphology.
source: These findings underscore the relevance of brain network organization in understanding the pathomechanistic link of MetS and brain morphology.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation summarizing the implications of the network topology analysis.

claim: The virtual histology analysis relies on post-mortem brain samples, potentially different from in-vivo profiles.
source: First, the virtual histology analysis relies on post-mortem brain samples, potentially different from in-vivo profiles.
evidence: The claim acknowledges a limitation of the virtual histology approach.

claim: The predominance of UKB subjects may bias the results.
source: In addition, the predominance of UKB subjects may bias the results
evidence: The claim acknowledges a potential limitation due to sample composition.

claim: Potential reliability issues of the cognitive assessment in the UKB need to be acknowledged.
source: and potential reliability issues of the cognitive assessment in the UKB need to be acknowledged (Gell et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim acknowledges a limitation supported by a citation to Gell et al., 2023.

claim: The cross-sectional design restricts the ability for demonstrating causative effects.
source: Lastly, the cross-sectional design restricts the ability for demonstrating causative effects.
evidence: The claim acknowledges a fundamental limitation of the study design.

claim: A characteristic and reproducible structural imaging fingerprint associated with MetS was identified.
source: In conjunction, a characteristic and reproducible structural imaging fingerprint associated with MetS was identified.
evidence: The claim summarizes a main finding regarding the brain morphological pattern associated with MetS.

claim: The pattern of MetS-related brain morphological abnormalities was linked to local histological as well as global network topological features.
